title: Public trust is built through everyday administrative encounters, but human-centred service strategies often stop before integration and feedback-driven improvement
source_unit: OECD, Serving Citizens 2026: Delivering Better Public Administrative Services
geography: OECD and partner countries, with government survey data collected in late 2024 and reported for the status as of November 2024

observations.period: 2024; public administrative-service experience and institutional interface

denominator.unit: OECD cross-country public administrative service framework

service_role.value: Administrative services include obtaining identity documents, registering births or deaths, registering to vote, requesting benefits, and applying for permits or licences

trust_route.value: The quality of administrative-service encounters affects access to programmes, exercise of rights, and perceptions of public institutions

user_satisfaction.value: About two-thirds of recent users in most OECD countries report satisfaction with their experience

observations.method: OECD review and original government survey of human-centred public administrative service management and delivery, supplemented by country practices and service-user framing.
observations.uncertainty: The report describes administrative systems and reported user experience; satisfaction is not a direct measure of access, equity, service quality, or causal trust formation, and the survey captures government-side implementation status rather than a common citizen panel.
observations.subgroup: People using benefits, identity, voting, licensing, registration, and other administrative services, including people navigating major life events.
observations.counterinterpretation: Moderately high satisfaction can coexist with exclusion, burdens, or low-quality outcomes for people who never reach the service or face more complex needs.

denominator.unit: OECD countries in the report's cross-country government survey frame

reform_strategy.unit: percent of OECD countries with a government-wide strategy addressing public administrative-service improvement

human_centre.value: Almost all strategies include objectives to make services human-centred

implementation_gap.value: Many strategies lack clear implementation plans, cost estimates, capacity analysis, and robust monitoring and evaluation arrangements

life_events.unit: percent of OECD countries that have begun designing or delivering services around life events

observations.method: Government questionnaire and comparative assessment of public administrative-service strategies, implementation arrangements, and life-event delivery practices.
observations.uncertainty: A strategy or life-event initiative indicates institutional intent or partial implementation, not integrated service receipt, reduced administrative burden, or better outcomes for all users.
observations.subgroup: Central and subnational public administrations, service designers, people navigating home moves, births, deaths, voting, benefits, permits, and other cross-agency events.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal strategies can provide a necessary coordination baseline even when costed plans or shared data are still incomplete; implementation may also vary by service and government level.

observations.period: 2024; integrated life-event services and data sharing

denominator.unit: OECD countries and common life-event cases in the report's comparison

integrated_cases.unit: percent of common life-event cases supported by integrated services across public agencies

website_guidance.unit: percent of life-event cases where guidance is grouped on a website but agencies do not share data

not_started.unit: percent of life-event cases where integration has not started

coordination.value: Among 22 countries implementing a life-events approach, 14 report coordination between relevant agencies to share user data

observations.method: Comparative review of nine common life events across 30 OECD countries, distinguishing integrated services, grouped information, and cases where integration has not begun.
observations.uncertainty: The reported cases are not a ranking of countries by service depth, and data sharing can create privacy, security, legal, and exclusion risks if governance and user control are weak.
observations.subgroup: People managing multi-agency life events, especially those with limited time, mobility, digital access, language access, or administrative capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Not every administrative process benefits from a life-event approach; some separation can protect privacy, accountability, or professional specialization.

observations.period: 2024; user feedback, performance data, and policy learning

denominator.unit: countries in the report's public administrative-service measurement frame

user_surveys.unit: percent of countries running user surveys about service experience and problems

performance_targets.unit: percent of countries setting and tracking performance targets for service-delivering agencies

improvement_use.unit: percent of countries using user feedback or performance data to improve services

policy_use.unit: percent of countries using user feedback or performance data to shape policy

observations.method: OECD government survey of user-feedback collection, service-performance targets, data use, public communication, and policy learning.
observations.uncertainty: Country-reported data-use practices do not establish the quality, representativeness, timeliness, or actual influence of feedback, nor whether data use improves user outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Service users, frontline staff, public managers, policy designers, and groups whose experiences may be missing from surveys or administrative data.
observations.counterinterpretation: Collecting and publishing feedback can improve transparency even when it is not yet routinely connected to service redesign or policy decisions.

observations.period: 2025; subgroup satisfaction and possible non-use exclusion

denominator.unit: OECD countries in the 2025 OECD Trust Survey public-administrative-service comparison

recent_user_satisfaction.unit: percent of recent public-administrative-service users satisfied across 34 OECD countries

discrimination_gap.unit: percentage-point satisfaction gap for recent users who report experiencing discrimination versus the OECD recent-user average

other_gaps.value: Recent users with low education, ages 18-29, financial concerns, and women report satisfaction around 2-5 percentage points below the OECD average

nonuse_boundary.value: Restricting the comparison to recent users excludes around 45% of respondents and may systematically omit people who avoid administrative services

observations.method: 2025 OECD Trust Survey comparison of recent public-administrative-service users, with subgroup analysis and an explicit non-user limitation.
observations.uncertainty: The reported subgroup gaps are descriptive and satisfaction is not service access or outcome quality; excluding non-users may understate barriers, but the report does not estimate the size or direction of that bias.
observations.subgroup: People reporting discrimination, younger adults, people with lower education, people with financial concerns, women, and people who did not use administrative services in the prior year.
observations.counterinterpretation: Recent users may be more engaged or more able to navigate services than non-users; lower satisfaction among users can indicate harder encounters, higher expectations, or more complex needs rather than a single service failure.

related_sources.claim: Official 80-page OECD report PDF and government survey results.
Official OECD DOI and publication citation.

boundary: This record adds the public-administrative interface between life-course needs and institutional delivery. It is a government-survey and comparative service-management assessment, not a citizen panel, causal evaluation, administrative burden experiment, or proof that digital integration improves trust or equity.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD publication page, executive summary, full report, and PDF were reviewed for public administrative-service scope, survey timing, strategy and implementation, life-event integration, data sharing, user feedback, performance targets, and policy-use measures.
